concept: Given an array of daily temperatures, return an array where each element tells how many days you must wait until a warmer temperature. If no future day is warmer, the answer is zero for that day.

solutions.label: Brute Force with Nested Loops
solutions.summary: For each day, scan all future days to find the first warmer temperature.

solutions.label: Monotonic Stack
solutions.summary: Use a decreasing monotonic stack of indices. When a warmer day is found, pop and compute the difference for each resolved day.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an array of integers representing daily temperatures. For each day, you need to find how many days you have to wait until a warmer temperature appears. If no warmer day exists in the future, the answer for that day is zero.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So for an input like 73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73, day zero has temperature 73, and the next day is 74 which is warmer, so the answer for day zero is 1. Is that correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. And a few clarifications: the array length can be up to thirty thousand, and each temperature is between 30 and 100 inclusive. You should return an array of the same length as the input.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What about edge cases? If the array is empty, do I return an empty array? And if all temperatures are the same, every position gets zero since no warmer day exists, right?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes to both. An empty input returns an empty output, and if no future day is strictly warmer, the value is zero.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Alright. So to summarize: given an array of temperatures, I return an array where each element is the number of days until a strictly warmer temperature, or zero if none exists. Let me start with a brute force approach.

sections.title: Brute Force with Nested Loops
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph BF["Brute Force: temps = 73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73"]
        S0["i=0, temp=73"]:::blue --> S0a["j=1: 74 > 73 ✓ → wait = 1"]
        S1["i=3, temp=71"]:::blue --> S1a["j=4: 69 < 71 ✗"]
        S1a --> S1b["j=5: 72 > 71 ✓ → wait = 2"]
        S2["i=6, temp=76"]:::blue --> S2a["j=7: 73 < 76 ✗"]
        S2a --> S2b["No warmer day → wait = 0"]
    end
    classDef blue fill:#60a5fa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is to use two nested loops. For each day at index i, I scan forward from i plus one to the end. The first day j where the temperature is strictly greater gives the answer as j minus i.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me walk through the example. At index 3 the temperature is 71. I check index 4 which is 69, not warmer. Then index 5 is 72, which is warmer, so the answer is 5 minus 3, which equals 2.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: At index 6 the temperature is 76. I check index 7 which is 73, not warmer. No more days exist, so the answer is zero.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of this approach?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: In the worst case, every day scans all remaining days, giving O of n-squared time. Space is O of 1 excluding the output array. Can I do better?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes. Think about what information you're recalculating. Is there a way to avoid re-scanning future days for every position?

sections.title: Monotonic Stack
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    subgraph MS["Monotonic Stack: temps = 73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73"]
        P0["i=0: push 0
Stack: [0]"]:::purple
        P1["i=1: 74>73, pop 0→ans[0]=1
push 1. Stack: [1]"]:::purple
        P2["i=2: 75>74, pop 1→ans[1]=1
push 2. Stack: [2]"]:::purple
        P3["i=3: 71<75, push 3
Stack: [2,3]"]:::purple
        P4["i=4: 69<71, push 4
Stack: [2,3,4]"]:::purple
        P5["i=5: 72>69 pop 4→ans[4]=1
72>71 pop 3→ans[3]=2
push 5. Stack: [2,5]"]:::purple
        P6["i=6: 76>72 pop 5→ans[5]=1
76>75 pop 2→ans[2]=4
push 6. Stack: [6]"]:::purple
        P7["i=7: 73<76, push 7
Stack: [6,7]
Remaining → ans=0"]:::purple
    end
    P0 --> P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P6 --> P7
    classDef purple fill:#a78bfa,color:#000

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can use a monotonic decreasing stack that stores indices. I iterate through the array once. When the current temperature is warmer than the temperature at the index on top of the stack, I pop and record the difference.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me trace through. I push index 0. At index 1, 74 is greater than 73, so I pop index 0 and set answer at 0 to 1 minus 0 equals 1. Then push index 1.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: At index 5, the temperature is 72. I pop index 4 since 72 is greater than 69. The answer at index 4 is 5 minus 4, which is 1. Then 72 is also greater than 71 at index 3, so I pop again. The answer at index 3 is 5 minus 3, which is 2.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: At index 6, temperature 76 causes me to pop index 5 and index 2, setting their answers to 1 and 4 respectively. After processing all days, indices still on the stack get zero since no warmer day was found.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great. And the complexity?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total operations are O of n. Space is O of n for the stack. This is a significant improvement over the brute force.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Nice work. Let's recap. The brute force uses nested loops with O of n-squared time. The monotonic stack processes each element at most twice, achieving O of n time with O of n space.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is that the monotonic stack lets us efficiently match each day with its next warmer day. Instead of scanning forward repeatedly, we resolve multiple waiting days the moment a warmer temperature appears.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. This pattern of using a monotonic stack to find the next greater element is very common in interview problems. Well done.
